explanation: Hydration is key! Remind them that water is the secret partner to make their expectorant actually work.

question: Why do we bundle maternal and neonatal health services together?

options.A: Midwives only work during the first week after delivery
options.B: It is cheaper for hospitals to buy medications in bulk
options.C: Newborns require the exact same medical treatments as adults
options.D: The health and survival of the mother and baby are directly linked

explanation: Spot on! Mum and baby are a team. Treating them together ensures nothing gets missed during these crucial early stages.

question: Why do inhaled anesthetic gases exit the body so quickly through the lungs?

options.A: They easily cross the tiny air sacs (alveoli) from the blood right into the lungs.
options.B: Inhaled gases bind tightly to red blood cells until reaching the lungs.
options.C: The kidneys cannot filter gases, so the lungs are the only option.
options.D: Lung tissue actively pumps anesthetic molecules out into the room air.

explanation: Once a patient stops breathing the anesthesia gas, the gas dissolved in their blood naturally crosses the thin air sac membranes when they exhale, clearing it out fast.

question: A patient keeps having seizures even after trying three different anti-seizure medications at maximum doses. What is the best next step to explore?

options.A: Discharging the patient to outpatient psychiatric care
options.B: Immediate cessation of all pharmacological treatment
options.C: Evaluation for possible resective epilepsy surgery
options.D: Switching to a fourth standard anti-seizure drug

explanation: When medications don't control the seizures, referring the patient to an epilepsy specialist center for surgical evaluation is a great next step.

question: Why is teamwork between a dietitian and a pharmacist so important for patient safety?

options.A: To calculate the exact financial cost of hospital meal trays
options.B: To determine when the patient is ready for hospital discharge
options.C: To decide which nurse will feed the patient during the shift
options.D: To prevent bad interactions between food and prescribed drugs

explanation: Certain foods can block or dangerously increase how medications work, making a joint review by dietitians and pharmacists super important.

question: When is ECMO (Extracorporeal Membrane Oxygenation) usually considered for a COVID-19 patient?

options.A: Immediately upon admission before trying simple nasal cannula oxygen
options.B: As the first-line treatment for all patients with a mild cough
options.C: When the patient is ready to be weaned off all breathing support
options.D: When conventional mechanical ventilation fails to maintain adequate oxygen levels

explanation: Spot on! ECMO is a major rescue therapy saved for the toughest cases where regular ventilators just aren't doing the job anymore.

question: If a hospital uses all its DRF cash to fix a broken generator, what happens first?

options.A: The hospital will immediately receive a large grant from the ministry
options.B: Patients will start buying cheaper drugs from the hospital store
options.C: The cost of electricity in the wards will drop significantly
options.D: The pharmacy will soon run out of money to restock essential drugs

explanation: That breaks the rule of ring-fencing! Without cash in the revolving account, new medicine orders can't be placed, leading straight to empty shelves.

question: Why does a patient with severe anemia often have a fast heartbeat (tachycardia)?

options.A: The lungs stop absorbing carbon dioxide properly
options.B: Blood vessels become strictly constricted throughout the body
options.C: White blood cells are attacking the heart muscle tissue
options.D: The heart pumps faster to make up for low oxygen carrying capacity

explanation: When red blood cells are low, your body doesn't get enough oxygen. To help out, the heart beats faster to pump the remaining cells around the body quicker. You've got this!

question: Why does functional decline in degenerative disorders often fluctuate day-to-day?

options.A: Immune systems fight off the genetic code
options.B: Therapists alter medications every morning
options.C: Genetic mutations change their sequence daily
options.D: Patients experience varying levels of fatigue and stiffness

explanation: Factors like exhaustion, muscle stiffness, and small changes in health can cause daily ups and downs in what a patient is able to do. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T17#GNS222_U4_T17_h2)

question: Why should the fluid bag be kept at a low height during a washout?

options.A: To ensure a gentle, low-pressure gravity flow into the bowel
options.B: To speed up the chemical reaction of the irrigating fluid
options.C: To prevent the fluid inside the container from evaporating
options.D: To allow the nurse to check the temperature of the solution

explanation: Keeping the bag low prevents high pressure, protecting the delicate walls of the patient's intestine from accidental injury.

question: An older adult started oxybutynin three days ago and is now suddenly confused and restless. What should you do?

options.A: Encourage the client to drink more caffeinated fluids
options.B: Report the acute cognitive changes to the prescriber
options.C: Document the findings and recheck the client next week
options.D: Apply a cooling blanket to lower the body temperature

explanation: Older adults are extra sensitive to these drugs in the brain. Sudden confusion is a red flag that needs the doctor's attention right away.

question: What grooming tip should a nurse give to a patient on long-term blood thinners?

options.A: Use an electric razor instead of a blade
options.B: Stop all dental hygiene care to protect gums
options.C: Avoid brushing teeth to prevent minor bleeding
options.D: Shave with a traditional straight razor daily

explanation: Electric razors are much safer because they prevent accidental nicks and cuts that bleed easily on blood thinners. Smart advice!

question: Which of these is a key nursing duty when it comes to pharmacogenetics?

options.A: Diagnosing inherited genetic disorders without medical supervision
options.B: Performing complex laboratory DNA sequencing procedures in the ward
options.C: Synthesizing customized pharmaceutical compounds at the bedside
options.D: Checking for gene-drug warnings and monitoring for side effects

explanation: Spot on, future nurse! You play a vital safety role by checking prescriptions against genetic guidelines and keeping a close eye out for side effects. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T5#GNS125_U1_T5_h7)

question: Why do the testes hang outside the main body cavity in the scrotum?

options.A: To shorten the length of the vas deferens tube
options.B: To allow easier passage of urine through the urethra
options.C: To protect the internal organs from high abdominal pressure
options.D: To keep sperm production at a slightly lower temperature

explanation: Brilliant! Sperm cells need a temperature slightly cooler than normal body heat to develop properly. The hanging scrotum acts like a natural cooling system.

question: What is the main job of red bone marrow?

options.A: Synthesizing the organic collagen matrix
options.B: Producing blood cells through hematopoiesis
options.C: Storing energy reserves as triglycerides
options.D: Releasing calcium ions directly into bone

explanation: Red marrow is our body's busy factory for making red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets. Excellent!

question: Why do patients with acute viral hepatitis develop jaundice (yellow eyes and skin)?

options.A: The gallbladder ruptures and releases stored bile directly into the abdominal cavity
options.B: Swelling in the liver blocks bile flow, causing bilirubin to back up into the blood
options.C: Red blood cells multiply too quickly for the bone marrow to keep up with them
options.D: The kidneys stop filtering waste products due to a sudden drop in blood pressure

explanation: When the liver is swollen, normal bile drainage gets blocked. This backs up yellow bilirubin pigments into the bloodstream, turning the skin and eyes yellow.

question: Which of the following is NOT a common challenge in community mobilisation?

options.A: Cultural resistance to new health ideas
options.B: Political interference from local figures
options.C: Guaranteed 100% funding and instant community obedience
options.D: Apathy and lack of initial interest from residents

explanation: Communities are rarely instantly obedient or fully funded; engagement is usually hard work filled with resistance and roadblocks. [learn more](GNS124_U4_T2#GNS124_U4_T2_h6)

question: Why are strong opioid painkillers usually avoided for routine home care after an abortion?

options.A: They carry high risks of sedation, nausea, and dependency
options.B: They permanently damage the lining of the stomach
options.C: They cause the uterus to stop contracting completely
options.D: They raise blood pressure to dangerously high levels

explanation: Routine cramps can usually be handled safely with milder drugs, sparing the patient from heavy side effects like sleepiness and nausea. Makes total sense!

question: What causes the vast majority of common upper respiratory infections like a simple cold?

options.A: Bacteria
options.B: Fungi
options.C: Parasites
options.D: Viruses

explanation: Common colds are usually caused by viruses (like rhinovirus). That is why taking antibiotics at the very start doesn't help—antibiotics kill bacteria, not viruses! Keep up the great learning.

question: As a nurse, what is one of your most important duties right before the patient goes for surgery?

options.A: Verifying that the informed consent form is signed
options.B: Teaching the patient how to change their wound dressing
options.C: Ordering a special post-operative hospital diet
options.D: Scheduling the patient's follow-up clinic appointment

explanation: Great job! Making sure the consent form is signed proves the patient understands the surgery, its risks, and has agreed to it before heading to the theater.

question: How is a therapeutic nurse-patient relationship different from a regular social relationship?

options.A: Social relationships have a strictly defined end date
options.B: Therapeutic relationships focus solely on the patient's needs
options.C: Social relationships require professional nursing accountability
options.D: Therapeutic relationships involve sharing equal personal benefits

explanation: A therapeutic relationship is all about the patient's healing. In a social friendship, both people share their personal lives equally, but nursing is strictly about the patient.

question: Which of these is NOT a common barrier faced by patients needing rehabilitation?

options.A: Physical barriers like stairs and narrow doors
options.B: Negative cultural beliefs and social stigma
options.C: Excessive availability of trained therapists in rural areas
options.D: High financial costs for care and equipment

explanation: Correct! Rural areas unfortunately suffer from a serious shortage of healthcare workers, not an oversupply of them.

question: A nurse is checking a patient with early liver failure for brain confusion. Which physical sign should she look for?

options.A: Sudden paralysis of the lower extremities
options.B: Involuntary flapping tremor of the hands (asterixis)
options.C: Rigid muscle spasms in the jaw
options.D: Inability to focus the eyes on bright objects

explanation: Asterixis (often called a 'liver flap') is a classic sign where the patient holds their hands out, and the wrists briefly flap downward due to toxin buildup.

question: Your patient just had surgery and has painful trapped gas. What is the best first nursing action?

options.A: Insert a rigid nasogastric tube immediately without a doctor's order.
options.B: Assist the patient to ambulate in the hallway or change positions in bed.
options.C: Instruct the patient to hold the gas in to prevent embarrassment.
options.D: Administer strong intravenous narcotics for pain relief.

explanation: Movement is medicine! Getting a post-op patient walking or shifting positions wakes up the bowels and helps release gas naturally.

question: What are the three core ingredients needed for valid informed consent?

options.A: Payment of all hospital bills in advance
options.B: Written signature from the village head and husband
options.C: Voluntary agreement, full information, and mental capacity
options.D: Verbal agreement witnessed by two police officers

explanation: For consent to be valid, the patient must agree freely, understand the risks and benefits, and be mentally capable of making the choice. [learn more](GNS216_U1_T8#GNS216_U1_T8_h4)

question: Why is it so important for a baby to latch wide onto the areola during breastfeeding?

options.A: It increases the total daily urine output of the infant
options.B: It prevents the baby from spitting up after meals
options.C: It forces the baby to sleep longer through the night
options.D: It prevents maternal nipple soreness and ensures milk transfer

explanation: A good, wide latch helps the baby get plenty of milk easily while saving the mother from cracked, painful nipples. Technique is everything!

question: Why is the scrotum located outside the pelvic cavity?

options.A: To allow easier access for lymphatic drainage
options.B: To protect the bladder from direct physical trauma
options.C: To shorten the pathway of the ejaculatory duct
options.D: To keep the testes cooler than core body temperature

explanation: Normal sperm production requires a temperature a few degrees lower than standard internal body temperature, which the hanging scrotum provides. [learn more](GNS216_U2_T2#GNS216_U2_T2_h2)

question: Why do nurses use geometric dilution when mixing creams?

options.A: To ensure an even and thorough blend of the active drug
options.B: To remove all the natural oils from the base vehicle
options.C: To speed up the drying time of the lotion on the skin
options.D: To make the final mixture change color as it mixes

explanation: Mixing equal amounts gradually keeps the active drug from clumping up in one spot. It's a neat little trick of the trade!

question: Which cells swallow trapped fats inside artery walls to help form fatty streaks?

options.A: Platelets
options.B: Macrophages
options.C: Fibroblasts
options.D: Red blood cells

explanation: Macrophages are our immune cleanup cells, but when they eat too much trapped fat in the arteries, they turn into foam cells and start plaque buildup.

question: What does viewing a patient in their social context primarily involve?

options.A: Isolating the patient from family members during treatment
options.B: Recognizing how relationships and living conditions affect health
options.C: Focusing strictly on the diseased organ and laboratory values
options.D: Prioritizing hospital policies over community traditions

explanation: Social context looks at the broader picture of a person's life, including family and living conditions, which deeply influence health outcomes. [learn more](GNS112_U2_T4#GNS112_U2_T4_h1)

question: Why are hospitals often shielded from vicarious liability when dealing with true independent contractors?

options.A: The hospital does not direct or control the daily details of their work
options.B: Independent contractors are forbidden by law from making clinical errors
options.C: Staffing agencies pay a special tax that waives all hospital legal claims
options.D: Independent contractors do not possess valid nursing license certificates

explanation: If a worker is truly independent and manages their own methods, the classic boss-worker control link isn't there, protecting the facility.

question: How should a nurse document what a patient says about experiencing abuse?

options.A: Write a generalized summary to protect family privacy
options.B: Use direct quotes from the patient and record objective physical findings
options.C: Leave the information out of the chart to prevent legal complications
options.D: Record only the nursing diagnosis without patient comments

explanation: Clear and factual is best! Using direct quotes and objective notes protects the patient and builds a reliable record for future care or legal needs.

question: What safety step is required if a patient experiencing cardiac arrest is lying in a puddle of water?

options.A: Turn off all nearby electrical appliances in the room
options.B: Double the number of chest compressions you deliver
options.C: Move the patient to a dry area and dry the chest
options.D: Place rubber mats under your own shoes while working

explanation: Water conducts electricity. Moving the patient to dry ground and wiping their chest ensures the shock goes through the heart, not out into the water.

question: Why must the healthcare team pause and provide manual ventilation between failed intubation attempts?

options.A: To allow the local anesthetic time to numb the vocal cords fully
options.B: To let the mechanical ventilator automatically calibrate itself
options.C: To cool down the laryngoscope light bulb so it does not burn tissue
options.D: To restore the patient's blood oxygen levels before trying again

explanation: Stopping to ventilate the patient prevents dangerous drops in oxygen saturation while the team regroups. [learn more](GNS213_U2_T16#GNS213_U2_T16_h4)

question: An exaggerated outward curvature of the thoracic spine is known as what term?

options.A: Lordosis
options.B: Scoliosis
options.C: Kyphosis
options.D: Atrophy

explanation: Kyphosis refers to the common hunchback curve of the upper back, while lordosis is an inward sway of the lower back. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T3#GNS222_U1_T3_h3)

question: How does team nursing differ from total patient care?

options.A: Total patient care involves no registered nurses at all
options.B: Total patient care is only used in surgical operating theatres
options.C: Team nursing uses a mix of different staff cadres to care for a group of patients
options.D: Team nursing requires one registered nurse to do everything alone

explanation: Well done! Total patient care means one nurse handles everything for a patient, while team nursing shares the workload among a group of mixed staff.

question: What are the tiny eggs of head lice that attach firmly to the hair shaft called?

options.A: Nits
options.B: Larvae
options.C: Spores
options.D: Pustules

explanation: Nits are the tiny, oval eggs that head lice cement securely onto individual strands of hair. [learn more](GNS112_U5_T5#GNS112_U5_T5_h5)

question: Why is it important to check both physical health and mental status when assessing sexual problems?

options.A: Physical illnesses and emotional stress frequently interact to impair sexual function
options.B: Physical causes are always temporary while psychological ones are permanent
options.C: Medical insurance will not pay for treatment without both evaluations
options.D: Psychological causes can never be treated with medication

explanation: The body and mind work as a team. Good sexual health needs healthy blood vessels, steady hormones, and peace of mind all working together.

question: Which laboratory sample is most commonly checked to confirm a lung fluke infection?

options.A: Cerebrospinal fluid
options.B: Sputum
options.C: Urine
options.D: Venous blood cultures

explanation: Correct! Looking at a sputum sample under a microscope to find the parasite's eggs is the standard way to confirm the diagnosis.

question: Which type of shock is directly caused by a massive loss of circulating blood volume?

options.A: Anaphylactic shock
options.B: Cardiogenic shock
options.C: Hypovolemic shock
options.D: Obstructive shock

explanation: Think of the prefix 'hypo' (low) and 'volume' (fluid). Hypovolemic shock happens when there just isn't enough fluid or blood left in the pipes, usually due to heavy bleeding or severe dehydration.

question: How do alcohol-based disinfectants actually kill germs?

options.A: Forming hard crystals inside the bacterial nucleus
options.B: Blocking the respiratory system of the patient
options.C: Dissolving cell membranes and denaturing proteins
options.D: Lowering the room temperature to freeze pathogens

explanation: Alcohol is a tiny powerhouse! It rapidly tears apart the outer fatty layer of the germ and scrambles its vital proteins so it can't survive.

question: Which of these is a classic sign of mastitis in a breastfeeding mother?

options.A: Foul-smelling brownish lochia
options.B: Localized breast redness, pain, and fever
options.C: Complete absence of milk production
options.D: Painless bilateral breast enlargement

explanation: Mastitis means the breast tissue is inflamed or infected. You'll usually spot a painful, red, warm area on the breast along with fever and body aches.

question: Why is it so helpful to introduce psychological support early after a degenerative diagnosis?

options.A: It helps patients adapt before severe cognitive decline sets in
options.B: It eliminates the need for any future medical interventions
options.C: It stops the physical degeneration from spreading to organs
options.D: It guarantees complete recovery from emotional distress

explanation: Starting early means patients can still clearly express their thoughts and take part in planning their own care. Great nursing insight to keep in mind!

question: Why is post-test counselling still very important for someone who tests negative?

options.A: To prepare them for inevitable immune system decline
options.B: To reinforce prevention strategies and help them stay negative
options.C: To counsel them on managing chronic medication side effects
options.D: To verify that they paid the laboratory testing fee in full

explanation: Brilliant! A negative result is a great teaching moment to talk about safe habits, PrEP, and keeping that negative status.

question: How do beta-blockers help a patient diagnosed with coronary artery disease?

options.A: By dissolving existing blood clots inside the narrowed arteries
options.B: By increasing the strength of every single heart contraction
options.C: By widening the peripheral blood vessels in the legs and arms
options.D: By slowing the heart rate and reducing the heart's oxygen demand

explanation: Beta-blockers block adrenaline effects on the heart, lowering heart rate and blood pressure so the heart muscle needs less oxygen. [learn more](GNS213_U1_T4#GNS213_U1_T4_h6)

question: What happens during a pharmacokinetic drug interaction?

options.A: One drug changes how the body absorbs, metabolizes, or excretes another drug.
options.B: The manufacturing company changes the active chemical ingredients.
options.C: Two drugs fight each other directly on the surface of the skin.
options.D: The patient develops an allergic skin rash from eating certain foods.

explanation: Think of pharmacokinetics as what the body does to the drug. If one drug messes with how the body handles another (like blocking liver breakdown), that's an interaction!

question: As a nurse, why do you need to monitor patients with digestive disorders very closely?

options.A: Digestive issues never change after admission
options.B: Intestinal tracts do not connect to other systems
options.C: The gut controls vital fluid and acid-base balance
options.D: Patients with gut problems refuse all medication

explanation: Spot on! The gut manages critical body functions like fluids and chemistry. When things go wrong there, the whole body feels it. You are getting the hang of this!

question: Which type of uterine fibroid is most likely to cause trouble with a fertilized egg trying to implant?

options.A: Intramural fibroids
options.B: Subserosal fibroids
options.C: Pedunculated fibroids
options.D: Submucosal fibroids

explanation: Brilliant! Submucosal fibroids grow right inside the main cavity of the womb, messing directly with the inner lining where pregnancy needs to begin. You've got this!

question: Which lab finding helps you spot Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) because it is usually missing in HHS?

options.A: Severe lack of fluid in the body
options.B: Presence of ketones and acidosis
options.C: Extremely high blood glucose levels
options.D: Altered level of consciousness

explanation: Great clinical thinking! DKA involves heavy fat breakdown that produces acidic ketones, whereas HHS spikes the sugar sky-high without major ketoacidosis.

question: Why can taking very large megadoses of fat-soluble vitamins be dangerous?

options.A: Fat-soluble vitamins are stored in the body and can accumulate to toxic levels
options.B: The body attacks fat-soluble vitamins as foreign bacteria and triggers shock
options.C: Excess fat-soluble vitamins instantly turn into dangerous trans fats
options.D: High doses immediately cause total kidney failure by dissolving water in blood

explanation: Spot on! Because fat-soluble vitamins get stored in our body fat and liver instead of being peed out, taking too many over time can build up to dangerous levels.

question: Why do hospitals nowadays rarely give whole blood to patients?

options.A: Whole blood carries no oxygen-carrying capacity
options.B: Patients usually only need specific blood components
options.C: Whole blood spoils within two hours of collection
options.D: Processing whole blood is too expensive for hospitals

explanation: Great job thinking like a clinician! Blood is separated into parts so patients get precisely what they lack—like just red cells or platelets—rather than getting components they don't need.

question: Which of these is NOT a good nursing action when managing an outbreak using incubation data?

options.A: Prescribing broad-spectrum antibiotics to every community resident
options.B: Calculating the probable exposure date for sick patients
options.C: Stocking adequate testing supplies for anticipated surges
options.D: Educating exposed contacts on why they need to monitor symptoms

explanation: Spot on! Giving out unnecessary antibiotics causes drug resistance. Nurses focus on tracking, educating, and supporting the community instead.

question: Why is keeping furniture in the same place important for someone with low vision?

options.A: It prevents dust from accumulating under heavy chairs
options.B: It ensures compliance with local fire safety regulations
options.C: It improves natural lighting inside the living space
options.D: It helps them navigate safely using their memory of the layout

explanation: When furniture stays put, individuals can use their memory of the room to walk around safely without bumping into unexpected obstacles.

question: Why is regular follow-up care essential for a patient recovering from hyperemesis gravidarum?

options.A: To monitor her weight, hydration, and lab values for stability
options.B: To measure the exact length of the baby using a tape measure
options.C: To make sure she is exercising at the gym twice a week
options.D: To change her prescribed prenatal vitamins every single week

explanation: Frequent checks allow healthcare providers to catch returning dehydration or weight loss early before hospitalization becomes necessary. [learn more](GNS226_U2_T012#GNS226_U2_T012_h7)

question: A patient is prescribed an inhaled bronchodilator and an inhaled corticosteroid. In what order should they take them?

options.A: Corticosteroid in the morning and bronchodilator only at bedtime
options.B: Both medications mixed together in the nebulizer at the same time
options.C: Corticosteroid first, wait a few minutes, then the bronchodilator
options.D: Bronchodilator first, wait a few minutes, then the corticosteroid

explanation: Open the door first! Taking the bronchodilator opens up the airways so the steroid that follows can travel much deeper into the lungs to fight inflammation.

question: Which statement about depression in older adults is FALSE?

options.A: It can severely reduce a patient's overall quality of life
options.B: It requires proper medical and nursing intervention
options.C: It can present as vague physical complaints and fatigue
options.D: It is a normal and expected part of getting older

explanation: Never think depression is just 'part of old age'! It's an illness that needs proper care. Keep this in mind for exams and ward practice.

question: What is the usual outcome after a drug successfully goes through Phase II conjugation?

options.A: The drug becomes much stronger and lasts longer in the fat tissue
options.B: The drug turns into a prodrug that requires more liver processing
options.C: The drug binds permanently to red blood cells for transport
options.D: The drug becomes completely inactive and ready for excretion

explanation: Once Phase II finishes adding that bulky water-soluble tag, the drug is safely deactivated and primed for prompt exit through urine or bile.

question: Which receptor on human cells does the COVID-19 virus (SARS-CoV-2) mainly attach to?

options.A: Angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 receptor
options.B: Insulin growth factor receptor
options.C: Beta-2 adrenergic receptor
options.D: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptor

explanation: Great job! The virus uses its spike protein to lock onto ACE2 receptors, which are found in large numbers in our respiratory tract. You've got this!

question: Why do clinics sometimes screen patients for genetic markers before prescribing risky drugs?

options.A: Proactively preventing severe adverse drug reactions
options.B: Lowering the financial manufacturing cost of brand-name drugs
options.C: Shortening the total recovery time for acute bacterial infections
options.D: Completely eliminating the need for routine blood tests

explanation: Spot on! Genetic screening lets us spot vulnerable patients early, stopping bad drug reactions before they ever happen. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T5#GNS125_U1_T5_h5)

question: Which lab results are most important for a nurse to check before starting a patient on anti-bleeding therapy?

options.A: Clotting profiles like PT, INR, and aPTT
options.B: Thyroid hormone panels
options.C: Fasting blood sugar levels
options.D: Routine liver enzymes only

explanation: Always check your patient's clotting baseline! Tests like PT, INR, and aPTT tell you how their blood is currently handling coagulation.

question: What is the main building block the body uses to make steroid hormones?

options.A: Glucose
options.B: Tyrosine
options.C: Cholesterol
options.D: Hemoglobin

explanation: Not all cholesterol is bad! Your body actually uses it as the foundational raw material to build important steroid hormones.

question: What is the ultimate goal of home health nursing?

options.A: Replacing all family involvement in patient care
options.B: Helping the patient achieve maximum independence
options.C: Transferring the patient to a permanent nursing home
options.D: Keeping the patient dependent on daily nursing visits

explanation: Home health nursing focuses heavily on empowering patients to manage their own care and daily routines safely. [learn more](GNS324_U1_T5#GNS324_U1_T5_h2)

question: What is the main foundation of public health when looking at nutrition?

options.A: High-dose antibiotic use
options.B: Regular surgical screening
options.C: Adequate nutrition
options.D: Frequent vaccination

explanation: Great job! Eating proper food gives the body the energy it needs to stay healthy and fight off sickness, which is why it forms the bedrock of public health.

question: Which of the following is NOT a direct cause of haemorrhage?

options.A: A ruptured internal aneurysm
options.B: A deep knife wound to the thigh
options.C: A bleeding stomach ulcer
options.D: Excessive red blood cell production

explanation: Having too many red blood cells (polycythemia) thickens the blood or increases volume, but it does not directly cause bleeding like a ruptured vessel or wound does. [learn more](GNS123_U3_T4#GNS123_U3_T4_h4)

question: How is home health care different from regular hospital care?

options.A: Patients have no role in deciding their daily routines
options.B: Care happens in a familiar environment controlled by the client
options.C: Nurses have constant access to complex surgical equipment
options.D: Physicians make hourly rounds to check on every patient

explanation: Great try! In home care, you step into the patient's personal space, meaning they have more say over their environment compared to a strict hospital ward.

question: Why must the nurse immediately label the specimen tubes at the patient's bedside?

options.A: To keep the synovial fluid warm in the room
options.B: To satisfy hospital room cleaning rules
options.C: To help the local anesthetic work faster
options.D: To prevent mixing up samples with another patient

explanation: Immediate labeling at the bedside ensures patient safety and guarantees that laboratory results match the correct client. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T8#GNS222_U1_T8_h5)

question: Why must a pharmacy balance full cost recovery with making drugs affordable?

options.A: To prevent private pharmacies from suing the hospital for unfair competition
options.B: To ensure the doctors receive a bonus for prescribing cheaper medications
options.C: To comply with international laws governing pharmaceutical manufacturing
options.D: To make sure vulnerable patients can still afford their essential treatments

explanation: If drug prices climb too high, everyday patients won't be able to buy them, which defeats the whole public health mission of our hospitals.

question: Why is the nurse's role so important when a patient is first told they might have cancer?

options.A: To determine the final pathological tumor grade
options.B: To perform surgical removal of the tumor mass
options.C: To prescribe and administer initial chemotherapy doses
options.D: To reduce anxiety and guide patients through complex tests

explanation: Finding out about cancer is super scary. Nurses step in as guides and educators to help patients understand tests and calm their fears.

question: Which symptom strongly points to an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?

options.A: Lower back or flank pain
options.B: Gradual weight loss over days
options.C: Excessive daytime sleepiness
options.D: Severe localized skin dryness

explanation: When red cells break down inside the body, the kidneys take a hit, which often shows up as sharp lower back or flank pain.

question: Why would you give a drug through an injection (parenterally) instead of having the patient swallow it?

options.A: It requires no special technical skill.
options.B: It achieves much faster drug absorption.
options.C: It is completely painless for the patient.
options.D: It has zero risk of local tissue damage.

explanation: You got this! Injections bypass the digestive system straight into the bloodstream or tissues, meaning the medicine gets to work much quicker.

question: What is the big difference in how our bodies handle bacterial STIs compared to viral STIs?

options.A: Viral infections only affect the skin, while bacteria only affect internal organs
options.B: Viral infections respond quickly to standard doses of penicillin
options.C: Bacterial pathogens cause visible lesions, while viruses never show any external signs
options.D: Bacterial infections are cleared with antibiotics, whereas viral infections stay in the body long-term

explanation: Antibiotics wipe out bacteria completely, but viruses like HIV or herpes stick around in the body. Great to keep this distinction in mind for your exams!

question: Which of the following is a clear indication for starting dialysis in acute renal failure?

options.A: Normal laboratory values for serum creatinine and blood urea
options.B: A mild and stable increase in the patient's daily appetite
options.C: A temporary decrease in blood pressure caused by mild dehydration
options.D: Severe and persistent hyperkalemia that resists medical treatment

explanation: Dangerous electrolyte imbalances like unmanageable high potassium are a primary reason to start urgent dialysis. [learn more](GNS213_U4_T6#GNS213_U4_T6_h7)

question: What is the most common type of uterine cancer?

options.A: Squamous cell carcinoma
options.B: Clear cell carcinoma
options.C: Uterine leiomyosarcoma
options.D: Endometrial adenocarcinoma

explanation: Brilliant! Endometrial adenocarcinoma makes up the vast majority of all diagnosed uterine cancers.

question: Which cancer is the most common among Nigerian women?

options.A: Liver cancer
options.B: Breast cancer
options.C: Cervical cancer
options.D: Ovarian cancer

explanation: Breast cancer is recorded as the leading malignancy among women in Nigeria and globally. [learn more](GNS321_U1_T1#GNS321_U1_T1_h2)

question: What is a key feature of algorithmic standing orders?

options.A: They apply only to surgical procedures performed in tertiary hospitals
options.B: They require the nurse to call a doctor before every single step
options.C: They contain blank spaces for the nurse to write their own drug dosages
options.D: They use decision trees with branching questions to guide clinical choices

explanation: Algorithmic standing orders guide the clinician through a series of sequential questions based on patient findings to arrive at the correct care plan. [learn more](GNS124_U6_T6#GNS124_U6_T6_h3)

question: Why can a long-lasting seizure harm brain cells?

options.A: The brain burns through oxygen and sugar faster than blood can supply them
options.B: Excessive GABA production causes neurons to drown in cerebrospinal fluid
options.C: Blood flow to the brain completely stops during the entire episode
options.D: The skull shrinks rapidly due to increased intracranial pressure

explanation: That's right! Continuous brain firing is hard work. It creates a massive energy demand, leading to oxygen shortage and exhaustion if not stopped.

question: In the HEADS adolescent screening tool, what does the letter 'S' stand for?

options.A: Skeletal strength
options.B: Sexuality
options.C: Sleep hygiene
options.D: Skin integrity

explanation: Spot on! In HEADS, 'S' stands for Sexuality (and Suicide), guiding the nurse to check in on relationships and reproductive health.

question: A patient arrives at the emergency unit in status epilepticus (a seizure that won't stop). Which drug class should be given immediately to halt it?

options.A: Succinimides
options.B: Broad-spectrum agents
options.C: Benzodiazepines
options.D: Hydantoins

explanation: In an emergency, drugs like diazepam or lorazepam (benzodiazepines) work super fast to calm the brain down and stop a prolonged seizure. Quick action saves lives!

question: What is the main job of Phase II drug-metabolizing enzymes?

options.A: Destroying harmful bacteria inside the gastrointestinal tract
options.B: Converting inactive prodrugs into active chemical compounds
options.C: Adding a chemical group to make drugs water-soluble for elimination
options.D: Pumping medications directly across the blood-brain barrier

explanation: Spot on! Phase II enzymes attach a special chemical tag to drugs so they dissolve easily in water and can be safely peed or pooped out. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T5#GNS125_U1_T5_h4)

question: Which service is typically offered by community groups like adult day care centers?

options.A: Respite and temporary relief for family caregivers
options.B: Inpatient surgical procedures for chronic conditions
options.C: Emergency ambulance transport during a stroke
options.D: Permanent residential nursing home placement

explanation: Adult day care centers provide a safe, fun space for older adults during the day, giving family caregivers a well-deserved break to rest or work.

question: What is the main operational strategy used for disease surveillance in Nigerian health facilities?

options.A: Federal Hospital Statistical Monitoring
options.B: National Emergency Health Record System
options.C: Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response
options.D: Community Primary Care Diagnostic Network

explanation: The IDSR strategy is the standardized framework used across Nigerian health facilities to detect and report priority diseases. [learn more](GNS313_U1_T19#GNS313_U1_T19_h4)

question: What is a key feature that makes a tertiary health facility unique?

options.A: It only handles uncomplicated outpatient malaria cases
options.B: It is the first point of contact in a rural village
options.C: It provides basic immunization only
options.D: It serves as a center for training and medical research

explanation: Tertiary hospitals (like our teaching hospitals) do double duty: they provide advanced patient care while training future healthcare heroes and conducting medical research.

question: Which body regulates the professional conduct and practice of nurses in Nigeria?

options.A: National Association of Nigerian Nurses and Midwives
options.B: Nigerian Medical Association
options.C: Federal Ministry of Health
options.D: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria

explanation: Spot on! The NMCN is the main statutory body that oversees nursing education and practice standards in Nigeria.

question: A patient is admitted after a long period of severe vomiting. Which acid-base imbalance are they most at risk for?

options.A: Metabolic alkalosis
options.B: Respiratory acidosis
options.C: Metabolic acidosis
options.D: Respiratory alkalosis

explanation: Stomach fluid is packed with hydrochloric acid. When a patient vomits it all away, they lose acid and retain excess bicarbonate, leading to metabolic alkalosis.

question: Why does the body use fibrinolysis after a blood vessel has finished healing?

options.A: To prevent the platelets from sticking to healthy tissue
options.B: To stimulate rapid production of new red blood cells
options.C: To trigger the initial vascular constriction phase
options.D: To remove the unnecessary clot and restore normal blood flow

explanation: Once the vessel repair is complete, the body doesn't need that old clot anymore. Fibrinolysis cleans it up so blood can flow smoothly again without blockages!

question: Why might a client with a true seizure disorder still have a completely normal EEG result?

options.A: The electrodes were placed on the wrong side of the forehead
options.B: Abnormal electrical activity may not happen during the recording period
options.C: The recording machine can only detect slow wave patterns
options.D: Anticonvulsant medications permanently cure abnormal brain waves

explanation: An EEG is just a snapshot in time. A patient can have epilepsy and still have a totally quiet, normal EEG when the machine happens to be recording!

question: What should you do right after a patient finishes their steam inhalation session?

options.A: Spray the patient's throat with strong antiseptics
options.B: Assist the patient in wiping their mouth and face
options.C: Immediately place the boiling jar into an ice bath
options.D: Seal the dirty water inside the jar for laboratory testing

explanation: Exactly! Gently wiping their face clears away any condensed moisture or medicine residue so it doesn't dry on their skin and cause irritation.

question: What does nutrient utilisation mean in the human body?

options.A: Storing excess fat directly beneath the skin layers
options.B: The rapid excretion of waste products through the kidneys
options.C: The physical chewing and swallowing of solid meals
options.D: Converting ingested food into energy and structural components

explanation: You've got this! Nutrient utilisation is simply how the body takes down food molecules and turns them into useful energy and building blocks for the body.

question: A manager watches a nurse perform a sterile dressing change to ensure correct technique. What type of control is this?

options.A: Feedforward control
options.B: Concurrent control
options.C: Financial control
options.D: Feedback control

explanation: Observing care as it happens lets the manager catch and fix mistakes on the spot. That's concurrent control!

question: Which of these is NOT something a nurse should do when dealing with harmful traditional practices?

options.A: Performing the harmful traditional practice to please community elders
options.B: Offering supportive counseling to women resisting the practice
options.C: Providing respectful health education on the dangers involved
options.D: Reporting illegal procedures or child abuse to the right authorities

explanation: As a nurse, your first loyalty is to your patient's safety. You should never take part in harmful traditional practices, no matter the local pressure! [learn more](GNS216_U1_T8#GNS216_U1_T8_h8)

question: What is the very first practical safety step before applying a prepared warm poultice to a patient?

options.A: Wrap the entire body in thick blankets
options.B: Test the temperature of the mixture
options.C: Leave the room for thirty minutes
options.D: Scrub the skin hard with stiff wire wool

explanation: Always test the temperature to prevent accidental burns before the substance touches the patient's skin. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h6)

question: On her third day after delivery, a patient complains that her right calf is painful, swollen, and feels warmer than the left. What is the most important thing you should do?

options.A: Encourage her to walk briskly around the hospital corridor
options.B: Massage the calf firmly to break up any muscle cramps
options.C: Apply an ice pack directly to the painful calf muscle
options.D: Instruct the patient to stay off her feet and notify the physician immediately

explanation: This sounds like a deep vein thrombosis (blood clot). Never massage a suspected clot, as it could break loose and travel to the lungs—always keep the patient resting and call the doctor right away!

question: Why doesn't full milk production start until after the baby and placenta are delivered?

options.A: The infant's cry is required to wake up the dormant pituitary gland
options.B: The mammary ducts do not form until the exact moment of birth
options.C: Prolactin is entirely absent from the maternal bloodstream until labor
options.D: High pregnancy hormones during gestation block full milk secretion

explanation: Spot on! While pregnant, high levels of estrogen and progesterone act like a block on full milk production. Once the placenta is out, that block is removed!
